paragraphs: The fungal kingdom is a vast and wild world. Scientists estimate that up to 12 million species remain undiscovered. Often called dark fungi, these microscopic or hidden organisms elude discovery but are all around us.

Although historically misclassified as plants due to their root-like networks, fungi are biologically closer to animals. Over a billion years, they evolved diverse ecological roles. Many form essential partnerships with plants as they exchange soil nutrients for carbon, a relationship that originally helped plants colonize land 470 million years ago. Other fungi produce complex chemical weapons like antibiotics or psilocybin to deter predators, while some, like Cordyceps, turn ants into zombies to spread their spores.

Remarkably, certain species thrive in extreme environments like Chernobyl. They use melanin to absorb harmful radiation and convert it into energy. Globally, vast underground fungal networks store massive amounts of carbon, which helps keep the planet resilient against climate change.

paragraphs: Fungi are a very large and special group of living things. This group includes mushrooms, yeast, and millions of other species. Fungi look like plants, but they are closer to animals. They do not get energy from the Sun; they eat other materials.

Fungi are very important to nature. They help plants grow. They give them food from the soil. Some fungi do strange things, like changing ants into zombies or smelling like bad meat. This way, they attract flies.
Other strong fungi can live in dangerous radioactive places like Chernobyl. Big fungal networks keep carbon underground. This keeps the planet safe from climate change.

paragraphs: The world of fungi is huge and surprising, and scientists think there are millions of undiscovered species.
For a long time, people thought fungi were plants because they grow in the soil. But they are closer to animals, and their cell walls are made of chitin, just like insects.

Fungi play many important roles in nature. Many plants cannot live without fungi, which give them nutrients from the ground. Some fungi use strong chemicals to protect themselves, like mushrooms with hallucinogenic molecules. Others are dangerous, like the zombie fungus, which controls the bodies of ants.

Amazingly, some fungi can even live in radioactive places like Chernobyl and use radiation as a source of energy. These underground fungal networks are very important for the Earth because they store carbon and protect our climate.
